name: Alexander the Great
role: King of Macedon (336-323 BC), hegemon of the League of Corinth and king of Persia
summary: A Macedonian king who conquered the Persian empire and pushed to the Indus, justifying the war as revenge for the Persian invasion of Greece and later claiming the kingship of Asia. He left no writings, so his views come from acts and from speeches and letters reported by later historians. He destroyed Thebes and Tyre, but also used local rulers and customs, adopted Persian court dress and ceremony, and married Persians and encouraged mass intermarriage at Susa. He sought honours above those of ordinary kings.

notes: No writings of his own survive. Arrian, Plutarch and Diodorus wrote centuries later from lost earlier accounts, so reported speeches (Hyphasis, Opis) carry the historians' wording and are used only at medium or low confidence. Quintus Curtius Rufus and Plutarch's 'On the Fortune or Virtue of Alexander' could not be fetched in this session. Persian dress, proskynesis and claims of divinity are reported with doubt in the sources; Arrian himself disapproves of several of these acts. Later pass 2026-11-13 (rules 7): sources tagged by evidence (the histories record his acts). McCrindle's compilation of Arrian, Curtius, Diodorus, Plutarch and Justin on the Indian campaign (Gutenberg 66388) is read by theme and cited for decide-locally (Nysa left free under its own laws; Taxiles and Porus kept as rulers); the Hyphasis mutiny and the Opis speech were already used from Arrian.
